analysis.one_liner: Exempts shipping to Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and territories from Jones Act rules unless three independent carriers compete.
analysis.headline: The bill to open island shipping routes to foreign competition has sat in a House subcommittee since January 2025 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jones Act requires ships moving goods between U.S. ports to be American-built, mostly American-owned, and American-crewed. That makes ships far more expensive to buy and run, and shipping to places like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico is dominated by a small number of carriers charging high rates. This bill would lift those requirements on island and Alaska routes — letting in cheaper foreign ships — unless at least three independent operators each already carry at least 20% of the goods on a route, which none of those routes currently meet [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. territories, who pay some of the highest freight costs in the country because the Jones Act's build-and-crew rules sharply limit the number and cost of ships serving them. Cheaper shipping would lower the price of imported goods on the islands [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts noncontiguous routes (trade involving Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories) from the Jones Act requirements that vessels be U.S.-built, at least 75% U.S.-owned, and mostly U.S.-crewed [S2] [S3].

The exemption only stays off if three independent operators each carry at least 20% of a route's volume — a level of competition that noncontiguous routes, served by a handful of Jones Act carriers, do not currently have [S2] [S3].
Lower shipping costs on these routes would translate into lower prices for everyday goods, since freight costs are built into the price of nearly everything island residents buy.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Jones Act fleet and the shipyards that build its vessels would lose protected, high-rate business on these routes, and American crews on noncontiguous runs could lose jobs to lower-wage foreign crews. Supporters of the current law also argue a domestic fleet and shipbuilding base serve national-security needs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act carriers and U.S. shipyards

drawbacks.text: The exemption would expose the domestic fleet serving these routes to competition from foreign carriers with lower-cost ships and crews, putting American maritime jobs and revenue at risk.

Reduced demand for coastwise-qualified vessels would shrink orders for U.S. shipyards, which critics say would weaken the domestic shipbuilding base that national-security advocates tie to the Jones Act.

The bill relies on a volume-share test — it only applies where fewer than three independent operators each carry at least 20% of a route — which would require ongoing monitoring of market shares and leaves edge cases, such as operators under common ownership, to be litigated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For island residents, the benefit is real and direct: shipping rates to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico are high largely because few expensive American-built ships serve them, and opening the routes to competition would pressure those rates down. The cost falls on a concentrated group — the Jones Act carriers and shipyards — plus some American maritime jobs, and there are legitimate national-security arguments for keeping a domestic fleet. The bill is drawn narrowly (it preserves the Jones Act wherever genuine competition already exists), which blunts the strongest objection that it is full repeal, but it does not address the domestic fleet's long-term viability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee in January 2025 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, joined by Rep. James Moylan, with two cosponsors in total [S1] [S3] [S4].

The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on January 23, 2025, and to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation the next day; the sponsor delivered introductory remarks on February 4, 2025 [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill has not received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and remains pending in the current Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill, which means the status quo holds: the Jones Act carriers serving Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico keep their protected routes and rates, and island consumers keep paying them. The bill could still move, but as of now the entrenched operators are the ones better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jones Act shipping operators, for now

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act and delivered introductory remarks on the measure.

for.name: Rep. James Moylan
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, adding a territory perspective to the bill.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Sam Graves, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at committee and subcommittee without a hearing or markup for the remainder of the session so far.

against.name: Jones Act shipping operators and domestic maritime industry
against.role: Coastwise carriers and shipyards (e.g., Matson, Pasha, Crowley, TOTE; American Maritime Partnership)
against.what_they_did: The domestic shipping industry has long opposed exemptions and repeals of the Jones Act, arguing they cost American jobs and weaken the U.S.-flag fleet.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has only three named supporters — a Hawaii Democrat, a Guam Republican, and one more cosponsor split between the parties — and no recorded opposition votes, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record yet.

industries.note: These carriers currently hold a legally protected position: the Jones Act bars foreign-built, foreign-crewed ships from hauling goods between U.S. ports, keeping rates high. The bill removes that protection on island and Alaska routes, so their interest runs directly against lower costs for island consumers.

The Jones Act's U.S.-build requirement funnels orders for expensive American-built ships to domestic yards. Exempting noncontiguous trade would cut that demand, and the yards' protected revenue comes at the price of higher shipping costs passed to the public.
If the exemption applies, foreign carriers could enter routes they are now barred from, and their ability to offer cheaper service is the mechanism by which island consumers would benefit.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to exempt or repeal the Jones Act have repeatedly died in committee, and this one has a single-digit cosponsor count and no hearing nearly a year into the session. The most likely path is that it stays in the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee and expires at the end of the Congress, though the Hawaii, Alaska, and territorial delegations could push for a hearing if shipping costs become a live political issue.
